I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over forty years. I know this soil, I know this climate, and I know what works. The North China Plain — this is wheat and corn country. That's what my father grew, that's what I grow, and I'm not about to change things at 68.

My land is about 15 mu. I'll put 12 mu into the winter wheat and summer maize double-crop rotation — the same land does both. After the corn comes off in late September, I rotate the soil with a machine cooperative's tiller and get the wheat in by mid-October. Come June, wheat is harvested, and I direct-seed corn into the stubble within a few days. The land is never idle. That's how we've always done it here.

I keep 3 mu near the house for vegetables — garlic, cabbage, some green beans. My wife manages most of that. We eat from it and sell a bit at Quzhou market. It's not a big earner but it keeps us fed and gives us something to do.

For seeds, I'll get the wheat variety the county extension station sells — they've been pushing Jimai 22 and it outyields the old stuff. For corn, hybrid seed is just what you use now. Zhengdan 958 or whatever the cooperative has in stock.

Fertilizer — I'll apply compound fertilizer at planting and urea as topdress for both crops. I don't measure it very precisely, I go by what's worked before and what my neighbors do. Three irrigations for wheat (before freeze, at jointing, at heading). Corn usually gets by on summer rain, maybe one irrigation if August is dry.

I hire the village machine cooperative for planting and harvesting — I can't do that myself at my age. I still handle the irrigation and spraying myself.
